title: Confirmation bias
body: We tend to seek and interpret evidence in ways that support existing beliefs.
apply: Look for the strongest evidence against your current opinion.

title: Cognitive dissonance
body: Inconsistent beliefs and actions can produce discomfort that motivates changes in behavior or interpretation.
apply: Notice when you are justifying a decision rather than evaluating it.
source: Festinger, A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance (1957)

title: Anchoring
body: An initial number can influence subsequent estimates even when it is irrelevant.
apply: Estimate the value independently before reading a quote.

title: Availability heuristic
body: Events that come easily to mind can seem more common than they really are.
apply: Check base rates before judging risk.

title: Framing effect
body: Equivalent outcomes can prompt different choices depending on how they are described.
apply: Rephrase a decision in terms of both gains and losses.

title: Sunk cost
body: Past unrecoverable investments can distort decisions about future spending.
apply: Ask whether you would start the project today at its remaining cost.
source: Arkes and Blumer, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes (1985)

title: Illusion of explanatory depth
body: People often overestimate how well they understand mechanisms until asked to explain them.
apply: Explain a familiar device step by step without looking it up.

title: Mere exposure
body: Repeated exposure can increase liking under some conditions.
apply: Distinguish familiarity with a brand from evidence of quality.
source: Zajonc, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1968)

title: Opportunity cost
body: Choosing an option means giving up the value of the best alternative.
apply: Compare a project's return with what the same time could earn elsewhere.

title: Theory of constraints
body: A system's throughput is often limited by a bottleneck.
apply: Find the step with the longest queue before adding resources.

title: Marginal analysis
body: Compare the additional benefit and additional cost of one more unit.
apply: Evaluate the next hour of work rather than the average hour.

title: Contribution margin
body: Revenue minus variable costs indicates how much a sale contributes toward fixed costs and profit.
apply: Calculate the margin of each service before discounting.

title: Economies of scale
body: Average costs may fall as output grows when fixed costs are spread across more units.
apply: Consider sharing equipment across compatible services.

title: Network effects
body: Some products become more useful as more people use them.
apply: Identify whether adding customers actually improves the product experience.
source: Katz and Shapiro, American Economic Review (1985)

title: Minimum viable product
body: An early product can test important assumptions with limited development effort.
apply: Test one useful feature before building a full platform.

title: Comparative advantage
body: Specialization can benefit both parties when their opportunity costs differ.
apply: Delegate based on relative costs, not simply who is best at each task.

title: Dichotomy of control
body: Stoic philosophy distinguishes our judgments and choices from external outcomes.
apply: Separate your next action from the result you hope to achieve.

title: Ship of Theseus
body: Replacing every part of an object raises questions about what makes it the same object.
apply: Consider what defines continuity during a renovation.

title: Veil of ignorance
body: Rawls asks us to imagine choosing social rules without knowing our own place in society.
apply: Design a policy as though you might occupy any role.
source: John Rawls, A Theory of Justice (1971)

title: Falsifiability
body: A scientific claim should expose itself to possible refutation.
apply: State what evidence would make you change your prediction.
source: Karl Popper, The Logic of Scientific Discovery

title: Burden of proof
body: A claim needs support; the absence of disproof is generally not evidence that it is true.
apply: Ask what independently testable evidence supports a claim.
source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Theories of Justification

title: Is–ought distinction
body: Descriptive facts alone do not establish what morally ought to happen without normative premises.
apply: Separate factual assumptions from values in a disagreement.
source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature, book III

title: Virtue ethics
body: Virtue ethics emphasizes character and practical wisdom rather than rules or outcomes alone.
apply: Ask which habit a repeated choice would cultivate.

title: Socratic questioning
body: Careful questions can expose assumptions and inconsistencies.
apply: Ask what a key term means before debating it.

title: Active listening
body: Listening to understand includes attending, reflecting and checking interpretations.
apply: Summarize what someone said before offering a solution.

title: Attribution error
body: Observers may overemphasize personal traits and underestimate situational influences, though patterns vary by context.
apply: Consider an alternative situational explanation before judging.
source: Ross, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology (1977)

title: Repair attempts
body: Attempts to de-escalate conflict can help partners return to constructive interaction.
apply: Acknowledge a harsh tone and restart the conversation.
source: Gottman and Silver, The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work

title: Emotional granularity
body: Distinguishing specific emotions may help people choose more appropriate responses.
apply: Replace 'bad' with a more precise description such as disappointed or anxious.
source: Barrett et al., Current Directions in Psychological Science (2001)

title: Responsiveness
body: Feeling understood, validated and cared for is important to relationship intimacy.
apply: Ask what support would feel helpful rather than assuming.
source: Reis and Shaver, Handbook of Personal Relationships (1988)

title: Self-disclosure
body: Mutual, appropriate disclosure can contribute to interpersonal closeness.
apply: Share a manageable detail and allow the other person to choose their pace.

title: Social support
body: Supportive relationships can buffer some effects of stress.
apply: Offer concrete help as well as emotional reassurance.

title: Perspective taking
body: Imagining another viewpoint can improve understanding but does not establish their actual thoughts.
apply: Check your interpretation with an open question.
source: Eyal, Steffel and Epley, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (2018)

title: Entropy
body: The total entropy of an isolated system does not decrease in ordinary thermodynamic processes.
apply: Notice why heat naturally flows from a warmer object to a cooler one.

title: Feedback loops
body: Negative feedback counteracts changes; positive feedback amplifies them.
apply: Think of a thermostat as a stabilizing feedback loop.

title: Nyquist sampling
body: A band-limited signal requires a sampling rate above twice its highest frequency for ideal reconstruction.
apply: Relate this to digital audio and anti-aliasing filters.

title: Packet switching
body: Networks transmit data in packets that can share communication links.
apply: Distinguish network congestion from a weak wireless signal.
source: Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach

title: Inverse square law
body: For an ideal point source in free space, intensity decreases with the square of distance.
apply: Doubling distance from an ideal sound source quarters intensity.

title: Natural selection
body: Heritable traits associated with reproductive success can become more common across generations.
apply: Distinguish population adaptation from individual acclimation.

title: Doppler effect
body: Relative motion changes the observed frequency of waves.
apply: Listen to a passing siren change pitch.

title: Redundancy
body: Independent backups can improve reliability, but shared failure modes undermine them.
apply: Keep a backup that does not depend on the original device.

title: Printing revolution
body: Movable-type printing existed in East Asia before Gutenberg's European system transformed book production.
apply: Consider how lower copying costs change access to information.

title: Antikythera mechanism
body: An ancient Greek geared device modeled astronomical cycles.
apply: Explore how mathematical knowledge can be embodied in machines.

title: Roman concrete
body: Some ancient Roman mortars contain lime clasts associated with self-healing mechanisms in laboratory experiments.
apply: Consider durability as a design goal, not just initial strength.

title: Standard time
body: Railroad coordination encouraged adoption of standardized time zones in North America in 1883.
apply: Imagine scheduling trains when every town kept its own time.

title: Rosetta Stone
body: The same decree in different scripts helped scholars decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs.
apply: Look for parallel examples when learning an unfamiliar system.

title: Transistor
body: The first working point-contact transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs in 1947.
apply: Trace modern computing back to the ability to switch and amplify signals.

title: Metric system
body: The metric system emerged from efforts to standardize measurement in revolutionary France.
apply: Recognize the coordination benefits of shared units.
source: NIST, History of the Metric System

title: Smallpox eradication
body: Global vaccination and surveillance led to WHO certification of smallpox eradication in 1980.
apply: Notice how coordinated monitoring complements a technical solution.

title: Implementation intentions
body: If–then plans connect a situation with a specific behavior.
apply: If I finish lunch, then I will spend ten minutes on one task.

title: Retrieval practice
body: Recalling information can strengthen later retention compared with simply rereading.
apply: Close a learning card and explain it from memory.

title: Spacing effect
body: Distributing practice over time often improves long-term retention.
apply: Review an idea tomorrow and again next week.

title: Interleaving
body: Mixing related problem types can help learners distinguish which solution applies.
apply: Alternate different kinds of practice problems.

title: Cognitive load
body: Working memory is limited; unnecessary complexity can interfere with learning.
apply: Break a procedure into steps and remove irrelevant details.

title: Attention residue
body: Thinking about a previous task can interfere with performance on a new one.
apply: Write a stopping point before switching projects.
source: Leroy, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes (2009)

title: Planning fallacy
body: People can underestimate completion times by focusing on ideal scenarios.
apply: Use actual durations from similar past projects.
source: Buehler, Griffin and Ross, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (1994)

title: Habit cues
body: Repeated behavior in stable contexts can become more automatic over time.
apply: Attach a small new habit to a reliable daily cue.

title: BATNA
body: Your best alternative to a negotiated agreement helps determine whether to accept an offer.
apply: Identify a realistic fallback before negotiating.
source: Fisher, Ury and Patton, Getting to Yes

title: Interests versus positions
body: A stated demand may hide a need that could be met in other ways.
apply: Ask why a deadline matters before bargaining over it.
source: Fisher, Ury and Patton, Getting to Yes

title: Common ground
body: Communication depends partly on shared knowledge and assumptions.
apply: Check that both parties mean the same thing by a technical term.

title: Teach-back
body: Asking someone to explain information in their own words can reveal misunderstandings.
apply: Ask a client to describe how they will operate a new system.
source: AHRQ, Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit

title: Nonverbal context
body: Nonverbal cues can provide context but do not reliably reveal a person's private thoughts.
apply: Verify an ambiguous expression rather than treating it as proof.
source: Hall, Horgan and Murphy, Annual Review of Psychology (2019)

title: Open questions
body: Questions that invite elaboration can elicit information missed by yes-or-no prompts.
apply: Ask what would make a proposal workable.

title: Information asymmetry
body: One party may possess relevant knowledge the other lacks, affecting decisions.
apply: Explain product limitations in terms a customer understands.

title: Integrative negotiation
body: Parties can sometimes create value by trading across issues they value differently.
apply: Explore timing, price and scope rather than only price.
source: Thompson, The Mind and Heart of the Negotiator
